plan.contextChunk: This figure places three small drawings in a row, each pairing a circle with a straight line rendered as a blue double-headed arrow, to enumerate how many points the two curves can share. In the leftmost drawing the circle is orange and the blue line passes above and to the left of it without ever touching the rim; the label beneath reads "No solutions." In the center drawing the circle is green and the blue line rises steeply from lower left to upper right, grazing the circle at a single point on its upper-left edge, which is marked with a filled black dot; the label beneath reads "One solution." In the rightmost drawing the circle is red and the blue line cuts through it, entering at the lower left and exiting at the upper right; the upper-right crossing is visibly marked with a filled black dot while the second crossing is implied by the line passing through the circle. The label beneath reads "Two solutions." The three panels hold the circle size and the line's slope fixed and change how far the line sits from the center, so the number of circle-line intersections is the variable. Together they lay out the complete range of outcomes for a system built from a circle and a line.

plan.concept: A line and a circle can intersect in zero, one, or two points, and the exact count is determined by whether the line’s perpendicular distance from the circle’s center is greater than, equal to, or less than the radius.

interactions.label: Line distance from center, d/r
interactions.teaches: As the same line slides parallel to itself, the number of shared points changes exactly when its distance from the circle’s center crosses the radius

interactions.label: Step through cases
interactions.teaches: The three possible systems are distinct: an exterior line has no common points, a tangent line has exactly one, and a secant line has two

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: The visual intersection count matches the algebraic discriminant: negative means no real intersections, zero means one tangent solution, and positive means two solutions

demo_steps.title: Exterior line: no solution
demo_steps.narration: The line misses the circle entirely. Geometrically, its distance from the center is larger than the radius, so the system has no shared point.

demo_steps.title: Tangent line: one solution
demo_steps.narration: Slide the line inward until it just touches the circle. At exactly d = r, the line touches the circle at one point, so the system has one solution.

demo_steps.title: Secant line: two solutions
demo_steps.narration: Move the line closer to the center. Once d < r, the line enters and exits the circle, producing two intersection points.

demo_steps.title: Connect the picture to algebra
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the equation view to see the same classification as a discriminant test after substituting the line equation into the circle equation.

plan.keyInsight: The number of solutions is controlled by one comparison: if the line’s distance from the circle’s center is greater than, equal to, or less than the radius, there are zero, one, or two intersections.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Use a clean horizontal three-panel layout inspired by the source figure: orange no-solution circle at left, green tangent circle in the center, red secant circle at right, each with the same steep blue double-headed line direction. In the interactive active view, keep the circle fixed and slide the line parallel to itself as the offset changes. Mark actual intersection points with filled black dots; show none for the exterior case, one dot for tangent, and two dots for secant. In equation mode, replace or accompany the drawing with a compact algebra panel showing circle plus line equations, the substituted quadratic, and a large discriminant sign matched to the current case: Δ < 0 for no solution, Δ = 0 for tangent, Δ > 0 for secant.
